subtype: Panic in a crowded or stressful place [Actor]
passage:
Dear Dolma,
You asked why I was so quiet on the phone on Monday. Here's the truth. On the 8:40 local to Churchgate, pressed between elbows and bags, I suddenly went hot all over. My fingers tingled, my chest locked tight, and every part of me screamed to get off, even though the train was moving. I honestly thought I'd faint.
Then I remembered what you told me after your exam-hall scare: breathe out slowly, hold something solid, and remind yourself it's a wave that rises and falls. So I gripped the metal pole, felt how cold it was, and counted my out-breaths. I told myself, this is the top of the wave. It will go down. By Dadar it had.
I'm going to see a doctor about it, like you did. Thank you for teaching me that.
Gautam

qa.a: Gautam felt terrified and trapped: hot all over, with tingling fingers, a locked chest and a desperate urge to get off.

qa.q: What helped Gautam ride out the panic until it passed?
qa.a: Slow out-breaths, holding the cold metal pole and remembering that the wave rises and then falls.

qa.q: How might Dolma feel reading the letter?
qa.a: Dolma may feel moved and glad that advice from Dolma's own exam-hall scare helped Gautam through it.

subtype: Panic in a crowded or stressful place [Actor]
passage: So, Tejas, you want the exam-hall story for the episode? Okay. Second-year finals, a hall with two hundred desks and none of the fans working. Ten minutes in, heat started in my neck and spread to my face. My hands tingled so much I dropped my pen. My chest felt like a belt was being tightened, and all I wanted was to run for the door. I'm Nikita, I'm usually the calm one, and I was sure I was about to faint in front of everyone. What saved me was simple. I pressed both palms flat on the wooden desk and felt its grain. I breathed out long and slow. And I kept telling myself, it's a wave, it peaks, then it drops. It peaked. It dropped. I wrote the paper. Afterwards I went to the campus clinic just to check, and they helped me find a counsellor.

qa.q: How many desks were in the exam hall?
qa.a: The hall had two hundred desks.

qa.q: What was Nikita afraid of during the exam?
qa.a: Nikita was frightened of fainting in front of everyone and desperately wanted to run for the door.

qa.q: Which actions helped Nikita stay and write the paper?
qa.a: Pressing both palms on the desk, breathing out long and slow, and remembering that the wave peaks and drops; later came a clinic check and a counsellor.

qa.q: How might other students in the hall have seen Nikita, if they noticed at all?
qa.a: They probably saw only someone pausing with hands flat on a desk, not the storm Nikita felt inside.

grounding: A young adult in an exam hall feels heat, tingling, a tight chest and an urge to escape, and gets through with slow breathing, touching something solid and remembering the wave passes.
